section_summary: This section (pages 664–732) contains State Department despatches, telegrams, internal memoranda, Military Intelligence Division reports, and FBI investigative surveys regarding Japanese political, economic, and foreign affairs between late 1940 and early 1941 (with retrospective memoranda into 1942). Key topics include the organizational structure and constitutional debates surrounding Prince Fumimaro Konoe's New Structure and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA), along with growing Diet, business, and public criticism of wartime economic controls and food rationing. The documents also examine deteriorating Japanese-American relations following Japan's adherence to the Tripartite Pact, unofficial peace missions and emissary proposals involving Count Yoriyasu Arima and Gracie Hall Roosevelt, rumors of an anti-war military coup d'état led by General Ugaki, and urgent recommendations for the evacuation of American citizens and missionaries from Japan.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file sheet noting Tokyo Telegram No. 1348 regarding the substance of the Japanese Foreign Minister's address at the America-Japan Society.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 1348, sent at 3 p.m. on December 19, 1940, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The telegram reported the substance of an address delivered by Japanese Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka at a luncheon of the America-Japan Society. The original paper is filed under decimal file 711.94/1884, with this cross-reference placed in the internal affairs file under 894.00/993.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Address of Foreign Minister at Luncheon of America-Japan Society

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Japanese press accounts of War Minister Tojo's meeting with army elders and allegations of Anglo-American interference in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Tokyo Telegram No. 73 summarizing Japanese vernacular press reports. The press highlights an unprecedented conference convened by War Minister Hideki Tojo with thirteen senior army leaders, including former War Ministers and Premiers, to explain the grave domestic and international situation and appeal for absolute military and national unity. The despatch also reports a Domei story from Hanoi alleging British economic rapprochement with French Indochina backed by the United States, as well as a Kokumin commentary citing Secretary Hull's interview with the Thai Minister in Washington as evidence of American interference in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 73: Summary Today's Press

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting a confidential conversation between an Embassy officer and Mr. Fujii, personal adviser to Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in Telegram No. 123 that Mr. Fujii, personal adviser to Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma, spoke confidentially with an Embassy staff member. Fujii emphasized a complete shift in Japan's internal political trends and conveyed the Japanese public's determination to pursue national leadership in East Asia at all costs. However, Fujii explicitly affirmed that neither he nor Baron Hiranuma had abandoned hope for improved relations with the United States, and he requested an immediate meeting with Embassy Counselor Eugene H. Dooman upon Dooman's arrival in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 123: Conversation with Baron Hiranuma's Adviser Fujii

subfiles.about: Telegram from Secretary of State Hull suggesting that further conversations with Baron Hiranuma's adviser Fujii might be productive.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sends Telegram No. 217 to the American Embassy in Tokyo referring to Tokyo Telegram No. 123 of January 27, 1941. Hull suggests that pursuing a conversation with Baron Hiranuma's personal adviser, Mr. Fujii, might be productive of helpful information if feasible and deemed appropriate within Ambassador Grew's discretion. The instruction was drafted in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and sent in confidential code.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 217 to Tokyo Regarding Conversations with Fujii

subfiles.about: Confidential State Department digest summarizing Tokyo Telegram No. 123 regarding statements by Baron Hiranuma's adviser Fujii.
subfiles.summary: This document provides a strictly confidential digest prepared in the Department of State summarizing Tokyo Telegram No. 123 of January 27, 1941. It records that Mr. Fujii, personal adviser to Baron Hiranuma, stated that although the Japanese people are prepared to go to the limit in pursuing their national policy of predominance in East Asia, neither he nor Hiranuma had abandoned hope of bettering relations between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.title: Digest - Telegram Received: Tokyo No. 123

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5268 on an editorial from the Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Herbert T. Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5268, which transmitted an editorial entitled 'The Year 1940' from the Japan News-Week, the only foreign-owned English-language paper in Japan. The memorandum notes that the editorial assesses the New Structure's elimination of liberalism, Japan's costly embrace of Nazi-Fascist ideologies at the expense of American and British friendship, and the ongoing economic drain of the China conflict. It underscores the editorial's warning that Japan is recklessly challenging the United States over issues outside her legitimate concern.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5268

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting and analyzing an editorial from the Japan News-Week reviewing Japan's totalitarian reorganization and international perils in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Despatch No. 5268 enclosing an extensive editorial entitled 'The Year 1940' from the December 28, 1940 issue of the Japan News-Week. Grew analyzes the editorial's critique of Japan's departure from traditional constitutional moorings into sweeping political, economic, and social totalitarianism. The enclosed text emphasizes the elimination of political parties and liberalism, severe regimentation of social and religious life, and the heavy unsolved burdens of the China Incident. The editorial strongly deplores the breakdown in Japanese-American relations following the Tripartite Pact, warning that Japanese leaders are gambling on a catastrophic conflict with the United States.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5268: Transmitting Japanese Press Comment: Editorial Entitled 'The Year 1940' from the Japan News Week of December 28, 1940

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting severe parliamentary criticism of the New Economic Structure and IRAA by Mr. Akaike and Prime Minister Konoe's reply.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports in Telegram No. 134 that Mr. Akaike, a member of the House of Peers, severely criticized the Government during a plenary session. Akaike demanded clarification on the failure of the New Economic Structure, alleged Marxist and Communist elements within economic controls, and the unsatisfactory nature of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe responded that wartime emergency demanded extreme control measures, insisted production expansion took precedence over ideology, denied the structure was Communistic, and explained the IRAA as an organ to link the Government and the people.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 134: Parliamentary Criticism of the New Structure and IRAA

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum evaluating unofficial Japanese peace overtures involving M. Kleiman, Count Arima, and the John Doe associates.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs submits a strictly confidential memorandum to Stanley K. Hornbeck analyzing seized Japanese Financial Committee records described by the Military Intelligence Division. Ballantine establishes that these records relate to 1941 rather than 1940. He points out that intermediary M. Kleiman counted on Count Yoriyasu Arima to arrange the dispatch of an unofficial American emissary to Japan, and that Tadao Wikawa (one of the 'John Doe' associates) identified himself as Arima's henchman. Ballantine concludes that both approaches originated from the same Japanese faction, which shifted its efforts entirely to the John Doe channel once Kleiman's overtures proved unproductive.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Regarding M. Kleiman and John Doe Peace Approaches

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reporting an impending Washington luncheon meeting concerning M. Kleiman's unofficial U.S.-Japan peace proposal.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton records that a luncheon meeting is scheduled in Washington involving M. Kleiman, the Japanese Financial Attaché in New York City, another Japanese representative, and several prominent Americans, including an associate or relative of President Roosevelt. The group intends to present a proposal for Sino-Japanese peace and improved American-Japanese relations, aiming to bypass the State Department by inducing the Americans to lobby President Roosevelt directly to send an unofficial emissary to Japan. Hamilton notes that Kleiman had previously approached the Department, which judged the scheme improper and unlikely to produce constructive results.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on M. Kleiman's Peace Proposal and Unofficial Emissary Project

subfiles.about: Memorandum examining file records of a proposed 1940–1941 mission by Gracie Hall Roosevelt to negotiate a settlement in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine reviews fragmentary file records regarding a 1940–1941 project for Gracie Hall Roosevelt, accompanied by Robert Barr Deans, to travel to Japan to negotiate a Far Eastern settlement with Japanese leaders. The records show discussions involving Japanese Financial Commissioner Juichi Nisiyama, Kamerman, Kleiman, J. M. Davies, General R. C. Marshall, and Colonel Sidney Mashbir. On January 15, conditions dictated to Nisiyama included a $50,000 fee plus travel expenses for Hall Roosevelt, along with a seven-point negotiation program. The venture apparently collapsed after Nisiyama disavowed any connection to the seven-point program.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Proposed Mission of Gracie Hall Roosevelt to Japan

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5315 regarding the organization of the IRAA.
subfiles.summary: Herbert T. Fales summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5315 regarding the administrative structure and regulations of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA). The memorandum details the supreme authority of the Prime Minister as President, the advisory bodies composed of Cabinet Ministers and Diet leaders, and the Secretariat's five functional bureaus. It also examines the Central and Prefectural Cooperative Councils designed to connect the government to the populace, observing that while the IRAA lacks a statutory foundation, an Imperial ordinance of December 26, 1940 placed it under Cabinet jurisdiction as its influence expanded over national life.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5315

subfiles.about: Extensive despatch transmitting detailed reporting, translated regulations, and structural diagrams of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides a comprehensive study of the origin, political character, and administrative machinery of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai). Grew traces the movement from Premier Fumimaro Konoe's August 1940 declarations through Count Yoriyasu Arima's Preparatory Commission, the inaugural gathering of October 12, 1940, and ongoing debates over constitutionality and relations with the Diet. Enclosure No. 1 provides a complete English translation of the seventeen articles of the Regulations of the Imperial Rule Assisting Movement. Enclosure No. 2 consists of detailed structural charts illustrating the hierarchy from the President and Advisory Body down through the Secretariat bureaus (General Affairs, Systematization, Policy, Planning, Diet) and the national and prefectural cooperative council networks.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5315: The Organization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5303 on the Bungei Shunju public opinion poll.
subfiles.summary: Herbert T. Fales summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5303 concerning a public opinion poll published in the January 1941 issue of Bungei Shunju magazine. The memorandum highlights that out of 685 predominantly white-collar respondents, 600 believed the public did not understand the New Structure, while 628 urgently demanded economic renovation. On the question of whether war between Japan and the United States could be avoided, 412 answered affirmatively and 262 negatively, with writers and journalists being the sole occupational group where a majority considered conflict unavoidable.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5303

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting and analyzing a ten-question public opinion survey from Bungei Shunju magazine regarding Japanese political, economic, and war attitudes.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on a public opinion poll conducted among 685 readers of the monthly magazine Bungei Shunju, representing government workers, professionals, and white-collar employees. Grew provides a detailed breakdown of responses to ten questions covering the New Structure, economic reform, war with the United States, youth ambition, stock speculation, radio programming, political leadership, careers in China, neighborhood leagues, and household income. The findings reveal widespread popular confusion and lack of enthusiasm regarding the New Structure, powerful sentiment for economic renovation (especially among Osaka merchants and farmers), dissatisfaction with aging political leaders, and a notable majority hoping that war with the United States can be averted.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5303: Poll of Public Opinion by the Bungei Shunju Magazine

subfiles.about: Letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmitting an intelligence report on Japanese conditions to Assistant Secretary of State Berle.
subfiles.summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation Director John Edgar Hoover writes to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr., transmitting data of potential interest. The transmittal forwards an investigative intelligence report originated by the FBI's St. Paul Field Office containing economic, military, and political information obtained from an American metallurgical expert who recently returned from Japan.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter Transmitting Japanese Intelligence Survey to Assistant Secretary Berle

subfiles.about: FBI intelligence report based on debriefings of metallurgical expert Louis H. Berry regarding Japanese steel, truck manufacturing, scrap shortages, and naval views.
subfiles.summary: Special Agent Benjamin J. Camp of the FBI St. Paul Field Office compiles an intelligence survey based on extensive interviews with informant Louis H. Berry, an American metallurgical expert who returned to the U.S. in December 1940 after eighteen months in Japan. Berry provides details on operations at the Nehon Spindle Company in Amagasaki (managed by Gumpei Kuwada and Vice Admiral Usui) and the Toyota Steel Company near Nagoya, which was producing 1,200 to 1,500 military trucks monthly and constructing new plants convertible to munitions. Berry emphasizes that the Japanese steel industry is critically hampered by American scrap iron embargoes, that Japan has only a sixty-day supply of gasoline, and that high naval officials, the Emperor, and the Premier strongly favored the United States over the Axis alliance, which was imposed by Army coercion.
subfiles.title: FBI Report: General Japanese Intelligence Survey (Interview with Louis H. Berry)

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting unverified intelligence of a planned military coup d'état led by General Ugaki to avert war with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports strictly confidential information from a source of uncertain reliability stating that an important group of Japanese Army officers and others proposed to overthrow the Konoe Cabinet by a coup d'état modeled after the February 26, 1936 incident. The conspirators allegedly argued that the current Government was leading Japan directly into a disastrous war with the United States. According to the informant, General Kazushige Ugaki had agreed to lead the movement, General Jinzaburo Masaki was designated Minister of War, and financier Seihin Ikeda had been approached to serve as Minister of Finance. Grew cautions that while the report cannot be verified and might be groundless, such an attempt was not impossible under present tensions.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 276: Reported Impending Military Coup d'État

subfiles.about: State Department paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 276 regarding rumors of an anti-war military coup d'état in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This document is an official State Department paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 276 of February 21, 1941, prepared in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs for secure transmission to the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Military Intelligence Division. It paraphrases the report that Army officers and civilian figures planned a coup d'état similar to the February 26 incident to remove the government and prevent a war with the United States, with General Ugaki leading, General Masaki as War Minister, and Seihin Ikeda approached for Finance Minister.
subfiles.title: State Department Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 276
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Military Intelligence Division

subfiles.about: Telegram from Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer requesting an urgent meeting with State Department Far Eastern officials following his return from Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer of the Board of Foreign Missions of the Methodist Church sends a telegram from Chicago to the Department of State, attention Stanley K. Hornbeck and Maxwell M. Hamilton. Diffendorfer reports that he has just returned from Japan and Korea, where Ambassador Grew expressed a strong desire that he confer immediately with State Department officials. He offers to spend the following Monday in Washington to discuss his findings.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ralph E. Diffendorfer Requesting State Department Conference
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation with Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer on totalitarian trends in Japan, German influence, Matsuoka's attitude, and missionary withdrawal.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine records a comprehensive conference between Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer of the Methodist Board of Foreign Missions and State Department officials Stanley K. Hornbeck, Maxwell M. Hamilton, and Ballantine. Diffendorfer recounts his impressions from visiting Japan and Korea, observing strong extremist control, pervasive totalitarian and youth mobilization, and growing German presence and influence. He describes a tense interview with Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, who warned the United States to stay on its side of the Pacific and declared Japan would never abandon China. Diffendorfer strongly advocates the immediate withdrawal of American missionaries and citizens from Japan, praising Consul General Marsh in Keijo for efficient evacuation handling and noting the persistent activities of German Jesuit priest Father Bitter in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum of Conversation: Dr. Diffendorfer's Impressions in Japan and Views on Evacuation

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Japanese press criticism of the Diet recess, IRAA shortcomings, Cabinet weakness, and Prince Konoe's leadership.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits Telegram No. 376 reviewing Japanese press commentary during the Diet recess. Vernacular newspapers heavily criticize the Government and Diet across four main themes: Diet opposition to the New Structure and IRAA exposing political disunity, the Government's failure to settle the vital China Incident while becoming distracted by secondary foreign entanglements, Prince Konoe's lack of aggressive leadership and persistent illness (suspected by some as political), and the overall weakening of the Cabinet. The press strongly urges fundamental Cabinet reorganization, either by adding ministers or establishing a streamlined 'war-time' cabinet with a revitalized Cabinet Planning Board.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 376: Press Criticism of Diet, Government, and Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Military Intelligence Division Report No. 10,257 on Japanese internal and foreign affairs.
subfiles.summary: Herbert T. Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Military Intelligence Division Report No. 10,257 of December 12, 1940. The memorandum outlines the appointment of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma as Minister Without Portfolio to reinforce the Konoe Cabinet, fierce business opposition to the Cabinet Planning Board's radical economic plan, proposed election law reforms establishing voter nominating councils, the reluctant acceptance of the Washington embassy by Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura, Foreign Minister Matsuoka's press statements regarding the Netherlands East Indies and Axis cooperation, and Japanese press condemnation of the U.S. loan to China.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on MID Report No. 10,257

subfiles.about: Extensive Military Attaché report analyzing Japanese domestic politics, military statements, Hiranuma's entry into the Cabinet, economic struggles, election reforms, rationing, Nomura's appointment, and Matsuoka's foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: The U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo submits Report No. 10,257 (Comments on Current Events - No. 39) evaluating critical domestic and international developments in Japan. The report reviews a joint Army-Navy declaration pledging total support for the New Structure and IRAA while urging national production expansion and suppression of impure political movements. It details Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma's appointment as Minister Without Portfolio alongside Naoki Hoshino, followed by a major political conflict between the Cabinet Planning Board and leading financiers under Baron Seinosuke Go over a drastic, allegedly confiscatory economic plan. The report also examines controversial election law amendments establishing voter councils and family-head voting criteria that threatened to disenfranchise prominent figures such as Minister Ishiguro and General Oshima. Finally, it surveys the widening rationing of food and consumer commodities, Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura's appointment as Ambassador to Washington, and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's press conference disclaiming territorial ambitions in the Dutch East Indies while reaffirming core alignment with the Axis.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Report No. 10,257: Comments on Current Events - No. 39
